To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the GnRH cell body is not the main site for GnRH secretion; 2) GnRH neurones are electrically coupled; and 3) GnRH neurone activity is patterned by a combination of electrical coupling, synaptic input and the intrinsic properties of the cells.
GnRH neurones have a unique cellular physiology that is different to that of all other neurones in the central nervous system.

GnRH neurones are capable of spontaneous action potential firing, which occurs in the presence of glutamate and in a Ca ^{2+} ‐dependent manner; GnRH neurones express voltage‐gated Ca ^{2+‐} channels and voltage‐gated Na ^{+} channels; the activity pattern of GnRH neurone firing is highly heterogeneous; and GnRH neurones exhibit a high level of electrical synchrony.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying GnRH secretion.
the cellular mechanisms that generate the pulsatile pattern of GnRH secretion.

the mechanisms that control pulsatile GnRH release, the mechanisms that underlie the generation of the GnRH pulse frequency, the mechanisms that control the timing of GnRH neuronal activity, and the mechanisms that control GnRH neuronal excitability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
GnRH neurones are not a homogenous population, that they are not a single type of neurones and that their activity is not a random process.
GnRH neurones are not intrinsically rhythmic, but that the GnRH neurone population is capable of generating a pulsatile output in a coordinated manner.
GnRH neurons are intrinsically capable of generating pulsatile activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the GnRH neurone is a highly excitable cell that is sensitive to the activity of neighbouring cells and to the activity of the GnRH neurones themselves, and is able to generate action potentials in a pulsatile manner.
the GnRH neurone is a unique and complex cell, and that the cellular events leading to the generation of GnRH pulses are not limited to the cell body, but rather involve the whole neurone.

pulsatile activity is generated by a network of GnRH neurone, and that the GnRH neurones are able to generate and maintain their own activity, but also that the network is able to adapt its function to external stimuli.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the GnRH neuronal network is a complex structure that can generate pulsatile activity in vitro, and that the GnRH network is not a passive structure, as it is capable of generating activity in the absence of synaptic inputs.
GnRH neurones are not simply ‘on’ or ‘off’ but are continuously active, with the frequency of firing being the main determinant of the amplitude of GnRH secretion.
the pulsatile GnRH release is the result of an interplay between the intrinsic properties of the GnRH neurone, and of the extrinsic inputs that it receives.
